stopBody: Its database binding and review settings are forgotten. Watching it again starts from the defaults.
intro: Snoutbot reviews the database change in a pull request against the database it is going to land on. Comment `@snoutbot review` on a pull request, or let it review every one that touches SQL.
pollHelp: GitHub cannot reach this computer, so SnoutData Studio checks for new pull requests and for `@snoutbot` comments every {seconds} seconds. Reviews happen while the app is running; closing the window keeps it in the tray, quitting stops it.
connectFirst: Connect a GitHub or GitLab account on the "Where your code lives" tab, and the repositories those tokens can reach appear here to pick from.
pickHelp: These are the repositories your token can reach. Pick one to start watching it, and it gets a card below where you choose the database its SQL is reviewed against. If one you expect is missing, the token's access is what decides, so widen it on GitHub.
askingWhich: Asking {forge} which repositories this token can reach…
allWatched: Every repository this token can reach is already watched
noReach: This token cannot reach any repositories.
noReachHelp: Snoutbot can only watch what the token can already see, so there is nothing to offer. Two things cause this:
cause1: It was not granted the repositories. A GitHub fine-grained token lists them one by one, and "All repositories" is not the default; a classic token needs the `repo` scope, and a GitLab one needs `{scope}`.
noScopes: No scopes are reported, which is normal for a GitHub fine-grained token and for GitLab: check the token was granted the projects you expect.
cause2: Your organization requires SSO and this token has not been authorized for it. Both hosts hide those repositories entirely rather than refusing them.
addByNameHelp: For a repository the list above cannot show, name it directly. Snoutbot still needs the token to be able to reach it.
repoPlaceholder: owner/name, or paste the repository URL
nothingWatched: Nothing is being watched yet. Pick a repository above, then choose which of your connections its SQL should be reviewed against.
identityYouWhy: A personal access token. No setup, and the comment carries your name.
identityAppWhy: A GitHub App in your own organization. Comments come from snoutbot[bot], and its key stays on this computer.
postedByThis: Reviews are posted by this account.
postsAs: Snoutbot posts as whoever the token below belongs to: as you, if it is your own token, or as a bot if you give it a bot's (see "Post as a bot" once it is connected). The token is kept {place} and never leaves this computer.
whatToAllow: What to allow on the token, and nothing else:

grants.repositoryAccess: the repositories you want reviewed, picked one by one. "All repositories" is not needed
grants.pullRequests: read the pull request, and post the review on it
grants.issues: read @snoutbot mentions in the conversation, and reply
grants.commitStatuses: show the review beside your CI checks, running then done
grants.metadata: name the repository; GitHub grants this automatically
grants.gitlabApi: read merge requests and post the review. The read-only scope could review and then fail to say anything

neverPushesGitlab: Snoutbot never pushes, merges or changes a branch. On a merge request it posts one note and edits it as the review changes, adds an emoji to the note that asked, and sets a status on the commit. The api scope allows more than that; GitLab has no narrower one.
neverPushesGithub: Snoutbot never pushes, merges or changes a branch. On a pull request it posts one comment and edits it as the review changes, adds a reaction to the comment that asked, and sets a status on the commit.
whichGitlabHelp: Your company's own instance, if you have one. The token below has to come from whichever GitLab this points at.
whyGithub: Why fine-grained, and what to do if your organization refuses it
whyGitlab: Why GitLab asks for so much
gitlabBroad: `{scope}` is a broad scope, and GitLab has no narrower one that can both read a merge request and post a note. That is the whole reason this token stays on your computer rather than being handed to a service.
fineGrained1: GitHub cannot pre-tick the fine-grained form from a link, so the permissions above have to be set by hand. If the repository belongs to an organization, an owner also has to approve the token before it works.
fineGrained2: It is worth the extra minute. The older `repo` scope is one switch that grants read and write to every repository your account can touch, now and in the future, including pushing code. Snoutbot reads pull requests, comments on them and sets a commit status.
fineGrained3Before: If your organization has not enabled fine-grained tokens, or you are on an older GitHub Enterprise Server, they are refused; a
fineGrained3After: is the fallback, with `repo`, or `public_repo` for public repositories only.
privateKeyKept: The private key is kept {place} and never leaves this computer.
appHelp: A GitHub App belongs to your organization, not to us. Create one, install it on the repositories Snoutbot should review, then give it its id and key here. Its comments come from `snoutbot[bot]`, and the key is kept {place}.
appStep1: Create the App, and give it these repository permissions:
appStep2: Generate a private key on its settings page. GitHub downloads a `.pem`.
appStep3: Install it on the repositories to review, then paste its App ID below.
notInstalledHelp: The credentials are right, so this is the last step: install the App on the repositories it should review. Until then there is nothing for it to look at, and nothing here will report an error.
botSummary: Post as a bot, not as you
botHelp: A comment is written by whoever the token belongs to. Neither GitHub nor GitLab lets a token post under a different name, so if reviews should come from "snoutbot" rather than from you, connect a token that belongs to a bot account. Nothing else changes: the review is the same, and Snoutbot still recognises its own comments.
botGitlab1: In the project (or group), open Settings, Access tokens.
botGitlab2: Create one with the `{scope}` scope and the Developer role. GitLab runs it as a bot user, so there is no second account to create.
botGitlab3: Disconnect above, and connect that token instead.
botGithub1: Create a second GitHub account for it, what GitHub calls a machine user.
botGithub2: Invite it to the repositories it should review, with write access.
botGithub3: Sign in as it, create a fine-grained token with the permissions listed above, then disconnect here and connect that token instead.
botFooter: Either way the review comment says who wrote it, in its heading and its footer, so it reads as Snoutbot's even while your name is on the byline.
connectionGone: That connection no longer exists. Pick another, or reviews stay text-only.
prodWarning: This is a production connection, so reviews now wait for you to read them before they post. Snoutbot only ever reads, and only ever counts (it never returns rows), but a staging copy of the same schema gives you almost every finding with none of the load.
runSqlOnly: On any pull request that touches SQL
deepConnected: Read the schema and measure the data
methodLocal: The rules, explained by the model on this computer
methodLocalNotInBuild: The rules, explained by the model on this computer (not in this build)
methodSnoutAi: The rules, explained by SnoutData AI
methodByok: The rules, explained by a model of my own
findingsSame: The findings never move between these. Every one of them is decided by the rules and measured against your database, whichever one you pick.
readBeforePost: Let me read the review before it is posted
waitsInApp: Reviews wait in the app until you post them, and the check on the commit stays amber while they wait.
postedDirect: Reviews are posted as a comment on the pull request as soon as they finish, and the check on the commit turns green or red. Snoutbot posts as you.
prodAlwaysWaits: A review against a production connection always waits for you, whatever this says.
reviewOutsiders: Also review changes from forks and outside contributors automatically
outsidersOn: Every pull request is reviewed on its own, including ones opened from a fork by someone who cannot write to this repository.
outsidersOff: Only changes from people who can write to this repository are reviewed on their own. Anyone else's waits until one of them comments a review command; comments from anyone else are ignored.
